title: Building a Multi-Class Application
summary: Structuring packages, coordinating collaborating services, and managing clean entry points.

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Modern International Airport

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: An international airport cannot function if luggage handlers are also piloting the Boeing 777, stamping passports at customs, and baking croissants in the terminal cafe. An airport operates through strict, specialized zones: 1) The Terminal Concourse (Presentation / CLI), 2) Security and Border Control (Validation / Gateways), 3) Air Traffic Control (Service Orchestration), and 4) The Fuel and Baggage Depots (Repository / Storage). Each zone interacts only through standardized communication channels.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In software engineering, professional multi-class Java applications are never jammed into one package or one file. They follow layered architecture: Domain Models (Entities & Value Objects) hold core state; Repositories abstract persistence; Services coordinate business transactions; and Controllers/CLI entry points handle user input. The 'Composition Root' in `main()` wires all layers together using Dependency Injection.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Divide multi-class applications into distinct layers: Domain, Repository, Service, and Entry Point.

activities.title: The Universal 4-Layer Architecture Pattern
activities.content:
### Layered Enterprise Architecture

```
[Presentation Layer (CLI / Web Controller)]
  │  - Parses user arguments and renders responses
  ▼
[Service / Application Layer]
  │  - Coordinates business workflows, transactions, and security checks
  ▼
[Domain Layer (Core Entities & Value Objects)]
  │  - Pure business logic, invariants, and domain calculations
  ▼
[Repository / Persistence Layer]
     - In-memory maps, file storage, or SQL databases
```

### The Composition Root Pattern
- The entry point (`public static void main`) acts as the **Composition Root**.
- It is the ONLY place in the application where concrete implementations are instantiated via `new` and wired together.
- Services and Repositories accept dependencies via constructors, never instantiating each other directly.

### Package Organization Best Practices
- `com.app.domain`: Entities (`User`, `Account`), Value Objects (`Email`, `Money`). Pure Java, no framework dependencies.
- `com.app.repository`: Interfaces (`AccountRepository`) and concrete implementations (`InMemoryAccountRepository`).
- `com.app.service`: Business coordinators (`TransferService`, `AuthService`).
- `com.app.cli`: CLI runners and terminal formatters.

activities.title: A Complete Layered Banking Transfer Application
activities.explanation: Demonstrates clean enterprise separation: BankAccount handles domain math, AccountRepository handles storage, TransferService coordinates transfers, and main wires dependencies.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `AccountRepository` defines storage contracts; `InMemoryAccountRepository` implements via Map.
`main` acts as Composition Root, wiring repo into service and executing transfer.

activities.title: Exception Handling and Domain Events Across Layers
activities.explanation: Illustrates domain exceptions and observer event listeners decoupled across collaborating enterprise services.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `InventoryService.deduct()` throws the checked domain exception when inventory is insufficient.

questions.question: What is the 'Composition Root' in a software application?
options: The root directory of the git repository
The unique centralized location (typically `main()`) where the dependency graph of the application is instantiated and composed
The java.lang.Object class
A database root table
questions.explanation: The Composition Root is where concrete implementations are instantiated and wired into service constructors at startup.

questions.question: Why should Domain Entities (like `Customer` or `Product`) avoid holding references to Repositories or UI components?
options: Domain entities should be pure, self-contained business models free from I/O, database, or presentation dependencies
Because entities cannot contain instance variables
Java does not allow entities to call other classes
It causes memory leaks in modern operating systems
questions.explanation: Domain entities should remain pure business logic, shielded from external infrastructure, storage, or presentation concerns.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of the Repository Pattern?
options: It encrypts all strings in bytecode
It abstracts data access behind an interface, allowing business services to work with domain entities without knowing whether they are stored in memory, files, or SQL databases
It forces all classes to be singletons
It speeds up JVM startup time by 50%
questions.explanation: Repositories decouple business services from database details, allowing easy swapping with in-memory doubles for testing.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Checked Exception and an Unchecked Exception in Java?
options: Checked exceptions extend `RuntimeException`; unchecked exceptions extend `Error`

Checked exceptions (extending `Exception`) must be declared in method signatures or caught at compile time; unchecked exceptions (extending `RuntimeException`) represent programming bugs and are not forced to be declared
Checked exceptions are faster than unchecked exceptions
Unchecked exceptions can only be thrown by the JVM itself
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions enforce compile-time handling for recoverable conditions, whereas RuntimeExceptions represent unexpected or illegal client conditions.

questions.question: What is 'Package-Private' access in Java and how does it protect multi-class module boundaries?
options: Methods marked with `private package` keyword
The default access level (no modifier), which allows classes within the same package to access members while hiding them from classes in outside packages
Access granted only to classes running in Docker containers
A deprecated feature from Java 1.0
questions.explanation: Package-private visibility hides internal implementation classes (like package helper classes) while exposing only the public interfaces to consumers.

questions.question: Why should business service methods accept Domain Objects rather than raw HTTP request / JSON string blobs?
options: To prevent buffer overflows in C++ libraries
Parsing and validating raw input belongs in the presentation/controller layer; service layers should operate on validated, type-safe domain entities
JSON strings cannot be passed across method calls in Java
It decreases the number of lines of code
questions.explanation: Separating input validation/parsing from business logic ensures that core domain services remain robust, type-safe, and transport-agnostic.

questions.question: What is an 'In-Memory Test Double'?
options: A duplicate CPU chip
A lightweight, in-memory implementation of an interface (like `InMemoryAccountRepository` backed by a `HashMap`) used to test services quickly without a real database
A thread that runs twice as fast
A clone of the JVM operating system
questions.explanation: In-memory test doubles implement repository interfaces using collections, enabling fast, isolated, deterministic unit tests.

questions.question: In a 3-tier architecture, in which direction should dependencies flow?
options: From Domain outward to UI and Database
From Presentation / Infrastructure inward toward Application Services and Core Domain
Circularly between all classes
Database directly into the UI views
questions.explanation: The Dependency Rule states that source code dependencies must only point inward toward higher-level domain policies.

questions.question: What role does the `java.util.Optional` class play in repository design?
options: It makes database connections faster
It explicitly signals that an entity might not exist (e.g. `findById`), forcing callers to handle the empty case and avoiding NullPointerExceptions
It allows arrays to resize dynamically
It replaces all if statements
questions.explanation: Returning Optional from lookup methods explicitly documents that a queried entity may be missing, forcing callers to handle that scenario safely.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to let Controller classes directly execute SQL queries?
options: Controllers cannot import java.sql.*
It violates separation of concerns, couples UI routing to database schemas, and makes testing business logic without a live database impossible
SQL queries run slower when called from controllers
Browsers reject responses generated with SQL
questions.explanation: Coupling controllers to database persistence destroys testability and spreads database schema dependencies throughout presentation code.

activities.title: FAANG Technical Interview: Multi-Class Application Architecture

questions.question: How do you organize a multi-module Java application to enforce clean architectural boundaries?
questions.answer: I organize into separate Maven/Gradle submodules: 1) `:domain` contains pure business models and repository interfaces with zero external framework dependencies. 2) `:application` contains business use cases and orchestrators. 3) `:infrastructure` contains database adapters, external HTTP clients, and AWS SDK integrations. 4) `:web` contains REST controllers and entry points. Because `:domain` has no dependencies on `:infrastructure`, developers physically cannot write SQL queries inside domain entities; the compiler enforces architectural discipline.
questions.keyTakeaway: Use build tool module boundaries to enforce unidirectional inward architecture.
keyPoints: Separate core domain from infrastructure using build modules
Prevent accidental leaking of database/HTTP logic into domain
Compiler enforces the Dependency Inversion Rule

questions.question: What is the difference between anemic domain services and rich domain models?
questions.answer: An anemic domain model has 'dumb' entity data bags with getters/setters and 'smart' procedural services executing all validations and calculations. This scatters business logic across services and makes invariants hard to protect. A rich domain model places business logic, invariant validations, and state transitions directly inside the domain entities (`order.applyCoupon(c)`, `account.debit(a)`). Services act merely as thin orchestrators loading aggregates from repositories, invoking entity domain methods, and saving results.
questions.keyTakeaway: Entities should guard their own invariants; services merely orchestrate workflows.
keyPoints: Rich entities own their state transitions and calculations
Thin services coordinate repository loading, transactions, and events
Prevents duplicate validation logic across multiple services

questions.question: How do you test a distributed transaction or multi-entity business workflow without spinning up slow test databases?
questions.answer: By relying on the Repository pattern and Dependency Injection. In our unit tests, we inject in-memory repositories (e.g. `InMemoryUserRepository` backed by `ConcurrentHashMap`) into our services. We can run 5,000 unit tests in under 3 seconds, testing error cases, timeouts, rollbacks, and concurrent race conditions deterministically. Real databases (PostgreSQL/MySQL) are tested separately in a smaller suite of end-to-end integration tests using Testcontainers.
questions.keyTakeaway: In-memory repository test doubles deliver blazing-fast, isolated unit testing for complex services.
keyPoints: Repository interfaces decouple services from concrete databases
In-memory implementations test transactions in milliseconds
Reserve live databases for a targeted integration test suite

questions.question: What is the Composition Root pattern, and where should it be located?
questions.answer: The Composition Root is the single point in the runtime execution graph where all concrete modules and services are instantiated and wired together. In a Java application, it resides at the application entry point (`public static void main` or the DI bootstrap configurator). Outside of the Composition Root, code should rely purely on interfaces and constructor injection, never using `new ConcreteService()` internally. This keeps the rest of the application completely decoupled and testable.
questions.keyTakeaway: Instantiate and wire concrete dependencies exclusively in the Composition Root.
keyPoints: Located at application entry point (main or DI configuration)
Rest of codebase relies on constructor-injected abstractions
Prevents scattered 'new' calls across business services

questions.question: When should you define custom Domain Exceptions vs using standard Java exceptions?
questions.answer: Standard exceptions (`IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`) are great for technical violations like null checks or out-of-range bounds. However, when a business invariant is violated that callers need to handle with specific business logic (e.g. `InsufficientFundsException`, `FlightOverbookedException`, `AccountSuspendedException`), defining custom domain exceptions allows callers to catch specific business failure modes and present tailored user error messaging or recovery workflows.
questions.keyTakeaway: Use custom domain exceptions for meaningful business failures that require distinct recovery.
keyPoints: Standard exceptions for technical programming errors
Domain exceptions convey business domain context
Allows specific catch blocks for tailored error recovery

questions.question: How do you handle domain events to decouple side-effects like sending emails or updating search indices?
questions.answer: We publish domain events (e.g. `UserRegisteredEvent`, `OrderPlacedEvent`) via an Observer / Event Publisher mechanism. When the core transaction completes, the service publishes the event. Independent event listeners (like `EmailNotificationListener`, `SearchIndexUpdater`, `MetricsEmitter`) receive the event and execute asynchronously or in separate threads. This keeps the primary order placement logic lean, fast, and completely unaware of downstream notification mechanisms.
questions.keyTakeaway: Domain events decouple primary transactions from secondary side-effects and notifications.
keyPoints: Primary business logic completes and emits domain events
Listeners handle secondary concerns (email, analytics, cache invalidation)
Promotes Single Responsibility and Open-Closed principles

practiceProblems.title: Warmup: Wiring Repository and Service in Composition Root
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
In the provided starter code, complete the `UserRepository` and `UserService` wiring in `main()`:
1. Model `User`: `id` (String), `email` (String). Getters.
2. Interface `UserRepository`: `void save(User u)`, `User findById(String id)`.
3. Class `InMemoryUserRepository implements UserRepository`: backing map `store`.
4. Class `UserService`: takes `UserRepository` in constructor. Method `String getUserEmail(String id)` delegates to repo.
In `main()` wire them together, save `User("U-1", "user@domain.com")`, and print the email.
hints: InMemoryUserRepository stores users in a Map<String, User>.

practiceProblems.title: Scratch: Modeling a Custom Domain Exception Pipeline
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a domain validation pipeline with custom exceptions from scratch without starter code:
1. Custom Exception `DuplicateUsernameException extends Exception`: message constructor.
2. Entity `Member`: `username` (String). Getter.
3. Service `RegistrationService`: private list of `registeredUsernames`. Method `void register(String username) throws DuplicateUsernameException`.
   - If username already exists in list, throw `DuplicateUsernameException("Username '" + username + "' is already taken")`.
   - Otherwise, add to list and print `'Registered: ' + username`.
4. In `Main`:
   - Create service
   - Register `'munaf085'` (succeeds)
   - Register `'munaf085'` again inside try-catch and print `'Caught: ' + e.getMessage()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Registered: munaf085
Caught: Username 'munaf085' is already taken
hints: DuplicateUsernameException is a checked domain exception extending Exception.
Catch the exception in main and print e.getMessage().

practiceProblems.title: Scratch: Domain Event Observer System
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a domain event publisher from scratch without starter code:
1. Interface `DomainEventListener`: `void onEvent(String topic, String payload)`.
2. Class `ConsoleAuditListener implements DomainEventListener`: prints `'[AUDIT] ' + topic + ': ' + payload`.
3. Class `EventPublisher`: private list of listeners. Methods `subscribe(DomainEventListener l)` and `publish(String topic, String payload)` which iterates and notifies all listeners.
4. In `Main`:
   - Create `EventPublisher`
   - Subscribe `ConsoleAuditListener`
   - Publish topic `'USER_LOGIN'`, payload `'User munaf logged in from 192.168.1.1'`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput: [AUDIT] USER_LOGIN: User munaf logged in from 192.168.1.1
hints: EventPublisher manages observer subscriptions and broadcasts events.
ConsoleAuditListener handles notifications decoupled from event sources.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Fixing Unhandled Missing Repository Entities
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
In the provided buggy code, `ProductService.getPrice()` directly accesses `repo.find(id).getPrice()` without checking if the product was found, crashing with `NullPointerException`!
Refactor the system:
1. Change `ProductRepository.find(String id)` to return `java.util.Optional<Product>`.
2. In `ProductService.getPrice(String id)`, if not found, throw `java.util.NoSuchElementException("Product not found: " + id)`.
3. In `main()`, catch the exception and print `'Caught: Product not found: PROD-999'`.
hints: Throw NoSuchElementException using orElseThrow() on Optional.

practiceProblems.title: Advanced: Complete Multi-Tier Order Fulfillment System
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a multi-tier order fulfillment system across 3 layers from scratch:
1. Domain Entity `OrderEntity`: `id` (String), `amount` (double), `status` (String: starts as 'PENDING'). Method `void markPaid()` sets status to 'PAID'. Getters.
2. Interface `OrderRepo`: `void save(OrderEntity o)`, `Optional<OrderEntity> find(String id)`.
3. Class `InMemoryOrderRepo implements OrderRepo`: uses `Map<String, OrderEntity>`.
4. Service `FulfillmentService`: takes `OrderRepo`. Method `boolean processPayment(String id)`: finds order, calls `markPaid()`, saves order, returns true; returns false if not found.
5. In `Main` (Composition Root):
   - Instantiate repo, add order `('ORD-1', 250.0)`
   - Instantiate service with repo
   - Call `processPayment('ORD-1')`
   - Print `'Order ORD-1 status: ' + repo.find('ORD-1').get().getStatus()` (PAID).
hints: FulfillmentService coordinates lookup, state change, and save.
